text: Mr. Hale, a retired teacher, stood in his hallway and looked at the dusty floor. "Hey phone," he said, "I do not want the big loud vacuum today. Send the little robot, and skip the bedroom." The assistant understood three things: use the smart robot vacuum, leave the bedroom alone, and keep the noise low. It sent the robot to the hallway, the kitchen and the living room, and it marked the bedroom as a room to avoid. Then Mr. Hale added, "Tell me when the bin is full. I may need to buy new filters." The assistant said it would send a message when the bin was full, and it put filters on his shopping list so he would not forget. Mr. Hale smiled, made a cup of tea and listened to the robot hum along the floor.

Grandpa Ron sat at the kitchen table with his tablet. He was a careful man, and the water bill had been on his mind all week. He typed quickly, with one finger: "when is my watr bill due". The assistant understood that he was asking about the water bill and looked up the date. "Your water bill is due on the twelfth," it said. "It is forty dollars." Ron wanted to stretch his money until the end of the month, so he typed again: "update my reminder to two days before". The assistant changed the reminder from the twelfth to the tenth and told him plainly that the old reminder was gone and the new one was set. Ron nodded. "Good," he said. "No more late fees." Then he finished his tea.

I want my parcel to be delivered at a different time.
Can you move my parcel to tomorrow at seven?
Deliver it later, please.
Not the usual time, make it after work.
Fix a new slot for my package, say Friday at noon.
My parcel was due on the third of April, but I will be out, so could it come the day after?
Reschedule the delivery.
Could you ask the courier to come later this week instead, since nobody is home before evening?
Push it back a day.
Hold the box until Monday morning and bring it then.

I want to send back something I ordered.
Return my shoes.
Send the blue jacket back.
Can I get my money back for the kettle?
I'm sorry to bother you, but the gas heater I ordered came with a broken knob, so could you please start a return and tell me where to drop it off?
Start a refund for order number 4471.
Rank the return choices for me, quickest first.
It doesn't fit, so I need to swap it for a bigger size.
Please take this back to the shop for me, I'm sorry, I just can't use it.

Mina owns a small shop that sells camping gear. On Friday morning she stood between the tents, holding a steel bowl she wanted to put on sale. A customer was planning a trip to the hills and asked what the weather would be. Mina did not want to walk to the back office, so she spoke to her phone. "Hills weather," she said. The assistant understood that she wanted the current weather in the hills north of town. It answered: cloudy now, ten degrees, with rain after four o'clock. Mina passed the news to the customer, who decided to leave early on Saturday. Then she said, "Rain jackets," and the assistant showed the jackets in her shop, with the number left in stock. Mina moved the three that were left to the front, next to the bowls.

Person: I want to post the video from my granddaughter's party.
Assistant: Which video do you mean? I found three from last weekend.
Person: The one where she sings her favourite song.
Assistant: Got it. Where should I post it, the family group or just one person?
Person: The family group, please. Is it long?
Assistant: It is twenty-five seconds long. Shall I post it now?
Person: Yes. And remind me about my doctor's appointment, I always forget.
Assistant: I posted the video to the family group. What day is the appointment?

A news feed is a short list of stories that your phone or speaker reads out each day. It is there so you can catch up in a few minutes while you sit with your breakfast. People change it to fit their day. If there are too many sports stories, they say, "Show less sport and more local news." If they only have a minute, they say, "Read just the headlines." Some people like to hear about a new movie on Fridays, so they say, "Add film news on Friday." To drop a topic, they say, "Stop showing weather in my news." Many people also change the time, with words like "Read me the news at seven" or "Send it later."

Priya got home after a night shift with heavy eyes and a weak voice. She dropped her bag by the door and said to her phone, "Anything in my email?" The assistant explained that she had a dozen unread messages and that three of them came from the hospital. It read the three aloud. One was from her manager about a change on Friday. "Tell her I will answer tomorrow at seven," Priya said, "and remind me then." The assistant did not send anything. It set a reminder for seven tomorrow morning and saved a short draft that said she would reply after her sleep. "Thank you," Priya said. She put the phone on the table and went to bed.

A table booking keeps a seat for you at a time you choose. It is useful because small restaurants fill up fast, and a Saturday night can be tight. Say you booked a table at the Busy Bee Cafe for four people. Later your plans change, so you ask for changes in plain words. You can say, "Make it five people." You can say, "Move it to eight o'clock," or "Can we sit outside?" If you want to cancel, you say, "Cancel my booking." On a phone you can just click the booking and pick a new time. Some people also ask for the menu or the hours, with words like "Are you open on Sunday?"

name: weekly_dinner_planner
does: Plans a week of dinners that fit what the family likes, and makes a shopping list for them.
inputs: how many people are eating, any foods to avoid, and how much time there is to cook
people say:
- What should we eat this week?
- My girl won't touch fish, so no fish dinners.
- It's foggy and cold, so plan warm meals for Monday to Wednesday.
- I need something quick on school nights, nothing over thirty minutes.
- Translate my wish for lighter food into a menu for five days.
- Fix me a dinner list for four people that doesn't cost much.

A bill is a request to pay for something you used, like electricity, water or rent. It has an amount and a due date, and paying late can cost extra. People change a few things about their bills. They set a reminder, move the due date, or choose to pay by the week instead of the month. Some banks round each payment up to the next dollar and save the difference, a little cushion like a soft pillow for the budget. To ask for these changes, people say things like, "Remind me three days before the rent is due," "Pay the water bill on the first," or "Round up my payments." If a bill is late, they say, "Pay it today."

Sun cream protects your skin from the sun at the beach. It is for the hours when you swim and play, and the sun is strongest at midday. Most people buy it at the pharmacy, and the number on the bottle tells how strong it is. A good rule is to put it on twenty minutes before you go out and again after you swim. People ask their phones to calculate the time. They say, "Remind me to put on sun cream every two hours," or "Tell me when the tide comes in." They also check the water: "How warm is the sea today?" Even a tiny change in the weather matters, so people say, "Check the sun strength again at noon."

I want to pay my yearly insurance bill early.
Pay the yearly insurance now.
While I brush my teeth, pay that insurance bill, and play a song when it's done.
Settle the annual insurance today instead of next month.
Can you take care of the insurance payment for this year before the due date?
Send the money for the one that comes once a year.
I'd like to pay it early, please, so I do not have to think about it later.
Pay it from my savings. Sorry, I mean from my checking account.
Do it now, no, wait, make it Friday.

Person: Cut the lawn shorter this time.
Assistant: How short? The mower is set to four centimetres now.
Person: Half of that, please.
Assistant: Two centimetres. Do you want me to start now?
Person: Yes, but keep the mower away from the flower beds. A little girl from next door left her toys there, and I want to hold off on that corner.
Assistant: I will skip the flower beds and the corner by the fence.
Person: Lovely. Can you also make the grass grow faster?
Assistant: I'm sorry, I can't do that. I can only cut it, but I can set the mower to run every three days instead of every week.
Person: Do that.

A smart speaker is a small box that listens for your voice and does what you ask. It is there to play music, answer questions and control things around the house. Most speakers use one account, but families can add more voices so the speaker knows who is talking. People change the volume all day. They say, "Turn it down," "Louder in the kitchen," or "Pull the volume back to low." They can group speakers with words like, "Play this in every room." A speaker is not the place to handle anything dangerous, like a fire or a bad fall. For that, people use the emergency number on a phone.

I want my coffee a little stronger.
Stronger, please.
Make my favorite coffee with two shots.
What happens if you use more beans? Do that.
Make it strong and put it on the bill.
Make it a bit stronger. No, wait, I mean tea, not coffee.
Less water in the cup so it is bolder.
Could you make it stronger and a little less sweet? Actually, keep the sugar the same.

Tom owns a wine shop with a small lawn behind it. On Tuesday morning he looked out of the window and said to his phone, "Start the sprinklers for twenty minutes." The assistant understood that he wanted the back lawn watered and set a twenty-minute timer. A minute later, Tom saw that the grass was still soft and wet from the night rain. "No, wait," he said. "Don't water today. Stop the sprinklers and try again on Friday." The assistant stopped the timer before the water started, then made a new one for Friday at the same time. It told Tom that nothing would run today and that the sprinklers were set for Friday morning. Tom thanked it and opened the shop.

Person: Hi, I just moved here and my wifi is slow. Can you switch me to the faster network?
Assistant: Sure. There are two networks, Home and Home Fast. Which one do you want?
Person: Home Fast. Sorry, no, wait, I think the guest one is the fast one. I'm not sure.
Assistant: The guest network is slow. Home Fast is the faster one. Should I switch to it?
Person: Yes. I have an online exam tonight and I can't be late.
Assistant: Done, you are on Home Fast now. Do you want me to check the speed again in an hour?
Person: Please do.

I want a longer bedtime story for my child.
Make the story longer.
One more story, please.
Double the length of tonight's story.
Download the one about the sour lemon so we have it in the car.
Can you forward the new story to Grandma's phone?
Keep going, we're not done yet.
Tell a story that lasts half an hour instead of ten minutes.

Rosa came in from the garden with dirt on her hands. The dishwasher had stopped again, and its little screen showed an error in German. "Translate this message," she said to her phone, and held the camera up. The assistant read the words and told her plainly that the filter was blocked. It said this problem is frequent when a dishwasher is used after muddy gardening gloves. Rosa laughed. She cleaned the filter, then said, "Run the dishwasher tomorrow at seven." The assistant set a timer so the dishwasher would start at seven in the morning, and it said so out loud. Rosa went back out to her tomatoes.

name: light_scene_manager
does: Saves, applies or deletes a named lighting scene, such as a dim movie setting.
inputs: the scene name, what to do with it, and which room
people say:
- Set up the laundry light so I can see while I load the washer.
- Delete the party colours from the living room.
- Turn the bedroom to full brightness for cleaning.
- Save this soft glow and call it reading time.
- Get rid of my old movie night lights.
- Put the lights back the way they were last night.

Ben, a student, was on the bus with his wireless headphones in and his eyes tired from a long night of reading. He typed in a hurry: "make the text biger and read my notes aloud". The assistant understood both parts. It raised the text size on his phone and began to read his notes in a clear voice through the headphones. A bush outside the window waved as the bus went round the corner, and Ben looked up. "Slower," he said. The assistant slowed the voice a little and kept reading from where it had stopped. Ben closed his eyes and listened until his stop.

I want the speaker to be louder.
Louder.
It's freezing on the porch and I can't hear, so turn it up.
Volume up a bit. No, sorry, I meant the kitchen speaker.
The ice machine is so loud that I can't hear the music, please raise the volume.
Keep turning it up until I say stop, and let the light on top flash when you can't go any higher.
Turn it up, but not that much, bring it back down two steps.

Sam, a student, was babysitting for the evening. At eight the baby was getting sleepy, but the blender was working loudly in the kitchen. Sam typed to the speaker in a hurry: "close the nusery blinds and start a nap timer for 40 minutes". The assistant understood that Sam wanted the blinds in the baby's room shut and a timer set for forty minutes. It closed the blinds, started the timer and said it would tell Sam when the nap was over. Sam turned off the blender, and the whole house went quiet.

Jess, a teenager, was stirring a pot of noodles while texting her friends. Her phone showed twenty-five missed calls, all from her grandmother. That was strange, so she said, "Call Grandma back on speaker." The assistant understood that she wanted to ring her grandmother and use the speakerphone so her hands stayed free. The call started. Grandma was in the attic, looking through old boxes on a cloudy afternoon, and her phone had been on silent. "I found your dad's baby photos," she said, laughing. Jess turned down the heat under the pot, read a quick message from a friend, and asked Grandma to hold up the pictures. The assistant kept the call going on speaker the whole time.

Dana finished her night shift and hung her coat on the hook by the door. Her friend Lee, a teacher, wanted to meet for dinner, but Dana was too tired to look for a place. She typed to her phone in a hurry: "book a tabel for two at the thai place tonight at 7". The assistant understood that she wanted a table for two people at the Thai restaurant she often visits, at seven in the evening. It checked and found the table free, booked it and told her the booking was for seven. It also said the kitchen stays open late, in case they ran behind. Dana sent Lee a quick message and slept on the sofa for an hour.

Omar was at his desk when he remembered that his mother, who lives alone, takes her pills at noon. "Mum's pills," he said quietly to his phone. The assistant understood that he wanted to know if she had taken them today. It checked her pill reminder and said she had confirmed the morning pills but not the noon ones. "Call her," said Omar. The assistant rang his mother. She had just come back from the garden and was making pancakes for the neighbour's children, and she took her pills while they talked. Before the call ended, Omar asked the assistant to set up a video call for Sunday, the kind they zoom on every week, so he could see her face.

Person: I want to read for half an hour every day.
Assistant: Sure. What time should I remind you?
Person: Tomorrow at seven, after dinner. Hold on, I'm slicing a cucumber for the salad right now.
Assistant: No problem. I set a daily reminder for seven in the evening, starting tomorrow. Is every day right?
Person: Yes. And charge my e-reader before then.
Assistant: I'm sorry, I can't charge it. I can remind you to plug it in at six, though.
Person: Do that, thanks.

I want to know when my food will arrive.
When is my dinner coming?
How long until the driver gets here?
It is thirty degrees outside and my ice cream may melt, so how many minutes are left?
Draw the driver's route on the map.
I'm sorry to bother you, but my phone battery is low and I have to leave soon, so could you please tell me how long the delivery will take?
Is it close yet?

name: next_bus_finder
does: Finds the next buses or trains from a stop and says how late they are running.
inputs: the stop or station, and the line if the person knows it
people say:
- When does the next bus come?
- Is the 8:15 train on time? I'm thirsty and want to buy a drink first.
- Translate this timetable into just the next three trains.
- I have no internet at home, how long will I wait at the corner stop?
- What time is the last tram tonight?
- Is my line running late?

Person: Make my letter shorter.
Assistant: By how much? It is about 400 words now.
Person: Make it half.
Assistant: I'll cut it to about 200 words. Do you want to keep the last paragraph?
Person: Yes, that is my favourite part. I've worked on this for an hour and I need a break.
Assistant: Done, it is shorter now. Do you want me to read it back to you?
Person: Not now. Can you send it to my boss?
Assistant: I'm sorry, I can't send it without an address. Who should get it?

Homework is work from school that students finish at home. It is for practice, and every task has a due date. Late work can make a teacher angry, so many students keep a planner on their phone or in a notebook. People change a planner all the time. They move a due date, add a new task or mark one as finished. They say things like, "Remind me to finish maths on Thursday," "Move the history essay to Friday," or "Close the science task, it's done." Parents use similar words: "What homework is due tomorrow?" Students who want to nail every deadline often ask the planner to remind them the night before.

Zoe was studying at her desk when the lights went out. The room was dark, the street was dark, and her phone battery was nearly empty. She was not scared, only worried about her laptop. "Power cut?" she said to her phone. The assistant understood that she wanted to know if the whole street had lost power. It opened the power company website and read out the notice: a cable had broken on her street and the power would be back in about two hours. "Please be patient," it added. Zoe thanked it. She saved her essay, turned on the phone light, and set an alarm for when the power was due back.

Carlos drives a delivery van, and on Saturday he was moving house. On Thursday night he stood among the boxes and said to his phone, "Don't book the big truck. I do not need two movers, just one." The assistant understood that he wanted a small van and a single mover. It cancelled the big truck and booked one mover for Saturday at nine. The dust from the old boxes made Carlos sneeze, and he asked about the weather. The assistant said it would be mild, about fifteen degrees, with no rain. Carlos put the last box in the back of his van. "Good," he said.

A bike ride tracker shows where you went, how far, and how fast. It is for people who want to see their progress, or plan a route before they leave. After a hot afternoon ride, many people fill the kettle and look at the numbers over tea. People change the settings in small ways. They say, "Plan a flat route of twenty kilometres," "Show my speed in miles," or "Avoid the busy road." They also say, "Tell me when I reach ten kilometres," so the phone speaks during the ride. If they get tired, they say, "Shorten the ride," and the route gets shorter.

Mrs. Ford, a retired teacher, stood in the garage with a bicycle that had a weak brake. She needed two new brake pads and was serious about spending no more than she must. The shop sold one pad for fourteen dollars. "What is twice fourteen?" she asked her speaker, and then, "And is that more or less than thirty?" The assistant understood that she wanted to double the number and compare it to thirty. It said that two times fourteen is twenty-eight, which is less than thirty by two dollars. Mrs. Ford started to smile. She wrote the number on the box lid, ordered the pads, and wheeled the bicycle back to the wall.

Nia had just moved to the city and knew no one. She spoke to her phone, politely: "Excuse me, I am new here and my legs feel weak after sitting at a desk all day, so could you please plan a medium workout for tonight? I would like something gentle that I can do at home." The assistant understood that she wanted a gentle, medium-level workout for home. It made a plan with three sets of ten squats, a short march on the spot and some stretching, with rests in between. Nia asked it to stream some music, and she did her first set on the carpet. Before bed she found a smooth stone in her pocket from the park near her new street, and put it on the shelf.

Leo, a student, sat in the cafe with a black coffee and checked his money. He typed in a hurry: "update my budget, spent 40 on bikee repair this week". The assistant understood that he wanted to record forty dollars for the bike repair under transport in his monthly budget. It made the update and then told him plainly that he had 120 dollars left to spend this month. It also said that this week was ten dollars more than last week. Leo sighed, finished his coffee and decided to walk home instead of taking the bus.

Hana was kneeling in the vegetable garden when she remembered her medicine. Her hands were muddy, so she did not want to touch her phone. "Pill time?" she said. The assistant understood that she was asking when her next pill was due. It answered that the next dose was at noon, in twenty minutes. Hana had been away from the kitchen since breakfast, and the pills were in her bag. "Make a note," she said. The assistant wrote down that she felt fine today and had not missed a dose this week. Her next task was to pick the beans, so she finished the row, washed her hands at the tap and took her pill at noon.

Voicemail is a place where a caller can leave a message when you cannot answer. It is for the times you are busy, away from your phone or asleep. People change a few things about calls. At night they put the phone on quiet so it does not ring. In a meeting they say, "Mute my phone," and later, "Unmute my phone." If they want others in the room to hear, they say, "Put the call on speaker." Many people ask, "Call my teacher back" or "Who called me today?" The phone can read out the missed calls and play each voicemail.

I want to pause my study timer for a while.
Pause the timer.
Hold on, I'm getting some ice for my drink.
It's rare for me to need a break, but I do now, so stop the clock for ten minutes.
Stop the study timer. No, make that fifteen minutes, then resume.
Resume the timer once I say I'm back.
Freeze my homework clock until I come back from lunch.
Could you stop counting? I'll tell you when to start again.

Ken works in an office with one big window. By two o'clock the sun was shining straight on his screen, and he could not read his list of payments. "Close blinds," he said to the speaker on his desk. The assistant understood that he wanted the blinds beside his desk shut, and it closed them halfway. It told him plainly that they were half closed and asked nothing more. Ken had eaten a grilled cheese sandwich for lunch, and now he checked the last payment on his list. It had to go out before five. The room was cooler and the screen was easy to read, so he finished the list by four.

I want to know when my flight leaves.
When does my plane take off?
Departure time?
Is my flight on time? It should be leaving in twenty-five minutes, I think.
What gate do I go to for the plane to Lisbon?
I want to win some time at the shops, so tell me how long before boarding starts.
Tell me if there is an extra delay.
Could you please check the board for me and read out the new time?
Will it leave later than planned?

Mia had worked all night and now wanted her hair done. Her friend had won a half price voucher for a salon, and it ended on Friday. "Book me a haircut," Mia said to her phone, "and I want pink at the tips." The assistant understood that she wanted a haircut with pink colour on the ends. It looked up the salon's opening hours and found a free place on Thursday afternoon at three. Because of the voucher, it said, the price would be half of the usual, about thirty dollars less. Mia said yes, and the assistant booked the visit and added it to her calendar. Then she texted her friend a thank you and went to sleep.

I want to see how much electricity I used.
Show me my power use for this week. No, I mean this month.
How much power did we burn today?
Give me the word on my energy use.
Deliver a short report of my electricity every Monday.
Tell me how much power the solar panels made. I paid a lot for them, so I want to know if they're worth it.
Is the house using less than last month?
Sorry, I meant yesterday, not today: what was the usage?

A contact is a card in your phone with a person's name and details. It is for finding people fast, so you do not have to remember every number. A contact can hold phone numbers, an address, a birthday and a short note. People change contacts all the time. They say, "Add Jo's new number," "Change Mum's address," or "Save this number as the plumber." They also say, "Remind me of Sam's birthday," and "Add a note to Dan: kind man, feeds my hamster when I travel." When a friend moves, you push the new address into the card, and the old one is gone.

Aziz, a cook at a small cafe, was ready for the morning rush. His tablet sat on its charging cable next to the digital scale. "Start twenty cups of strong tea," he said. Then he stopped. "No, wait. Make it coffee, not tea. The cafe sells more coffee on Mondays." The assistant understood the change. It dropped the tea order and started the coffee machine for twenty cups, strong, with no sugar. It said plainly: tea cancelled, coffee started. Aziz weighed the beans on the scale and put out the cups.

I want to know if the house has a leak.
Is there a leak anywhere?
Check the pipes for me.
There is water on the driveway up to the tire of my car, and I am afraid of a flood, so please check the water meter and tell me whether it keeps running.
Is water running when nobody is using it?
Shut off the water if you find something.
Is the water flow stronger than usual tonight?
I'm sorry, but I've been away all week and I'm worried, so could you please look at the water use and see if anything looks strange?

Mr. Okafor, a retired teacher, stood at the open fridge making lunch. "Excuse me," he said to his speaker in a soft voice, "would you please stop reading the sports stories? My grandson is asleep in the next room, and I would like only the local news, a little quieter." The assistant understood that he wanted fewer sports items, only local headlines and a lower volume. It stopped the sports, lowered its voice and read three local headlines: a new bus stop, a bake sale, and road repairs on Elm Street. Mr. Okafor nodded, took the cheese from the fridge and listened while he cut his bread.

name: resume_listening
does: Finds where you stopped in a podcast or audiobook and plays on from there, at the speed you like.
inputs: the title or the person who reads it, and how fast to play
people say:
- Where was I in my book?
- Pick up the story my favourite artist reads.
- Go on with last night's episode, but a bit faster.
- Which chapter did I leave off at?
- Feed me the next episode when this one ends.
- It's important to me to finish the book this week, so start where I stopped.
